title: How Lewis and Clark Worked
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss the Lewis and Clark expedition (the Corps of Discovery, 1804-1806), from Jefferson's motivations and the Louisiana Purchase through training, the Missouri River journey, Fort Mandan and Sacagawea, the Rocky Mountains, the Columbia River, the Pacific coast and Fort Clatsop, the return trip, and the aftermath, including York's treatment, Meriwether Lewis's disputed death, and manifest destiny. The episode opens with banter and a sponsor read, and closes with a listener mail from Jasper in Amsterdam about a Dutch arrest of a Russian diplomat and diplomatic immunity.
topics: Ken Burns Lewis and Clark documentary

segments.title: Sponsor read and opening banter
segments.summary: A Toyota Corolla sponsor read opens the episode, followed by casual banter about Clark's name, the explorers' personalities and writing, and watching the Ken Burns documentary.

segments.title: Louisiana Purchase and Jefferson's motivation
segments.summary: The hosts explain how the Louisiana Purchase from France, negotiated by Monroe for about fifteen million dollars, doubled the country's size and prompted Jefferson to send an expedition to survey the new land and look for a water route to the Pacific.

segments.title: Choosing Lewis and Clark and Lewis's training
segments.summary: Jefferson chose Meriwether Lewis, his secretary, who picked William Clark as co-captain. Lewis received crash training in science and medicine at the American Philosophical Society in Philadelphia. The hosts also discuss Lewis's depression and the rumors about his sexuality, with no evidence supporting them.

segments.title: Crew members, York, and Seaman the dog
segments.summary: The hosts describe the expedition's members, including York, Clark's slave who was a full party member and useful in diplomacy, the Newfoundland dog Seaman, and the discharge of men for misconduct early on.

segments.title: Departure from St. Louis and Missouri River travel
segments.summary: The expedition wintered near St. Louis, began in spring, and traveled upstream on the Missouri River, hauling boats against the current. They encountered the Teton Sioux, who demanded a canoe, and Chief Black Buffalo defused a standoff.

segments.title: Great Plains and Fort Mandan
segments.summary: The party reached the Great Plains, saw abundant wildlife, and built Fort Mandan near the Mandan and Hidatsa villages, where they spent the winter in friendly relations.

segments.title: Sacagawea, Charbonneau, and translation
segments.summary: The hosts describe hiring the trapper Toussaint Charbonneau and his wife Sacagawea, a Shoshone woman who served as translator and whose presence signaled peace. She gave birth to Jean Baptiste, who was later adopted by Clark. She also retrieved records from a capsized boat. The journals spell her name variously.

segments.title: Syphilis, sexual encounters, and Lewis's journal
segments.summary: The hosts mention venereal disease among the expedition members after encounters with Native women and Lewis's sparse, snide journal entries on the subject.

segments.title: Wildlife, grizzly bears, and the Three Forks
segments.summary: The expedition encountered prairie dogs, elk, buffalo, antelope, and grizzly bears. They reached the fork in the Missouri and followed the route the group's majority disagreed with, then crossed the Continental Divide and found the Three Forks, naming them after Gallatin, Madison, and Jefferson.

segments.title: Shoshone reunion and Bitter Root Mountains
segments.summary: Lewis located the Shoshone, and Sacagawea recognized a childhood friend and met her brother, now chief. With guide Old Toby, they crossed the Bitter Root Mountains, eating horse meat. Later they went down the Columbia River and left their horses with the Nez Perce.

segments.title: Reaching the Pacific and the vote on winter camp
segments.summary: The expedition reached the Pacific in November 1805, with Lewis writing it was tempestuous and horrible. Sacagawea, who wanted to see the ocean, came along to see a beached whale. The party held a vote on where to camp, including York and Sacagawea, and chose the south side of the river, where they wintered at Fort Clatsop.

segments.title: Return journey, Blackfeet conflict, and separation
segments.summary: The party headed home in March 1806, retrieving sunken canoes and trading for horses. In July they split up. Lewis was accidentally shot by Pierre Cruzatte, and the Blackfeet had a violent encounter where two died. The party reunited and John Colter left to explore Yellowstone.

segments.title: Aftermath, York's treatment, and Lewis's death
segments.summary: The expedition returned to St. Louis in September 1806 to cheers. Members received land and pay, but York and Sacagawea got none, and York's request for freedom was refused. Clark later had York flogged. Lewis became governor, then died in 1809 at Grinders stand in Tennessee from gunshot wounds, with disputed suicide or murder accounts. The hosts discuss manifest destiny and the fates of the members.

segments.title: Listener mail: diplomatic immunity
segments.summary: Jasper in Amsterdam writes about the Dutch arrest of a Russian diplomat for abusing his children, the Russian protest, and the Dutch government's apology based on the Vienna Convention's immunity rules.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank Jasper, invite listener email and social media contact, point to the website for more on Lewis and Clark, and close with a sponsor line for the Toyota Corolla.
